title: Using the right material: why a spoon is steel and a raincoat is plastic

summary.text: A paper spoon goes soft in wet food, so most spoons are steel. A raincoat must keep water out and bend when you move, so many raincoats are plastic. Your child makes spoons from newspaper and card, tests them against a steel spoon, and wraps biscuits to see which material keeps the rain out.
summary.art: A girl at a kitchen table holding up a floppy newspaper spoon in one hand and a shiny steel spoon in the other, with a bowl of water and a bowl of curd in front of her.

intro.hook: We eat with steel spoons, not paper spoons. We wear plastic raincoats, not paper raincoats. Why?
intro.text: Everything is made of a material. Wood, metal, plastic, glass, cloth and paper are materials. Each thing has a job to do. A spoon carries food. A raincoat keeps you dry. People choose a material that can do the job. In this unit you test spoons made of different materials, and find out which one lasts.
intro.art: A mother holding up a steel spoon and a child's yellow plastic raincoat, while a small girl looks from one to the other with a puzzled face.

outcomes: By the end I can say the job a thing does and the material it is made of.
By the end I can say why a spoon is usually made of metal: it stays stiff and does not soak up water.
By the end I can say why a raincoat is often made of plastic: it keeps water out and it bends.
By the end I can test spoons made of different materials, and say what I saw.
By the end I can say why water makes paper go soft.

terms.meaning: A material is what a thing is made of.
terms.example: A spoon can be made of steel, wood or plastic. These are three materials.
terms.art: Three spoons in a row: a shiny steel spoon, a brown wooden spoon and a red plastic spoon.

terms.meaning: The job of a thing is what we use it for.
terms.example: The job of a spoon is to carry food to your mouth. The job of a raincoat is to keep you dry.
terms.art: A spoon carrying rice to a child's mouth, and a child in a raincoat in the rain.

terms.meaning: Waterproof means water cannot get through.
terms.example: A plastic raincoat is waterproof. Rain runs off it, and you stay dry inside.
terms.art: Raindrops running down the outside of a yellow raincoat, with a dry child inside.

terms.meaning: To absorb means to soak up. A material that absorbs water drinks it in.
terms.example: A cotton towel absorbs the water on your hands. Paper absorbs water too, and goes soft.
terms.art: A cotton towel drying a child's wet hands, with the towel going darker where it is wet.

terms.meaning: Stiff means it does not bend when you push it.
terms.example: A steel spoon is stiff. It does not bend when you stir thick curd.
terms.art: A steel spoon standing straight in a bowl of thick white curd.

terms.meaning: Flexible means it bends easily without breaking.
terms.example: A raincoat is flexible. It bends when you lift your arms or sit down.
terms.art: A child in a raincoat stretching both arms up, the raincoat folding at the elbows.

explanations.concept: Every job needs a material that suits it
explanations.context: This card says how people choose a material for a thing. It is what the spoon test showed.
explanations.definition: People choose a material that can do the thing's job, again and again, without going wrong.
explanations.description: First ask what the thing must do. A spoon must carry wet food and stay stiff. A towel must soak up water. A material that is right for one job can be wrong for another.
examples: A towel is made of cotton cloth, because cloth absorbs water.
A window is made of glass, because you can see through glass.
A chair is made of wood, steel or plastic, because they are stiff and strong.
explanations.art: Three things with their jobs drawn beside them: a towel drying hands, a window with a tree outside, a chair with a child sitting on it.

explanations.context: This card explains why the newspaper spoon and the card spoon went soft in the spoon test.
explanations.definition: Paper and card are made of tiny threads from plants, called fibres. Water gets in between the fibres, and they stop holding each other tightly.
explanations.description: Tear a piece of paper slowly. At the torn edge you can see tiny hairs. These are the fibres. When paper is dry, the fibres hold on to each other, so it is stiff. When water soaks in, it gets between them and they let go, so the paper goes soft. Steel does not soak up water, so water cannot get inside it.
examples: A paper boat goes soft in a puddle after a few minutes.
A wet paper bag tears easily.
A cardboard box left in the rain goes soft and bends.
explanations.art: A close look at the torn edge of a paper, with tiny hair-like fibres sticking out, and a drop of water soaking in between them.

explanations.concept: Why a spoon is made of metal
explanations.context: This card says why most spoons in Indian kitchens are steel. It follows the spoon test.
explanations.definition: Most spoons are made of steel, a metal, because steel is stiff and strong, and it does not soak up water.
explanations.description: A spoon goes into hot rasam, thick curd and soapy water every day. Steel does not go soft, bend or crack, and it lasts for years. A thin plastic spoon can bend in very hot food. Wood is used for some spoons because it stays cool in the hand.
examples: A steel spoon in a tumbler of hot payasam stays stiff.
A long steel ladle stirs a big pot of sambar.
A wooden spoon is used to stir food in a non-stick pan, because it does not scratch.
explanations.art: A steel spoon in a bowl of hot payasam with steam rising, next to a wooden spoon in a pan.

explanations.concept: Why a raincoat is made of plastic
explanations.context: This card says why raincoats are made of plastic. It follows the Biscuit in the Rain activity.
explanations.definition: Many raincoats are made of plastic, or of cloth with a thin layer of plastic or rubber on it, because plastic is waterproof and flexible.
explanations.description: A raincoat has two jobs. It must keep the rain out, so it must be waterproof. It must bend when you walk and lift your arms, so it must be flexible. Plastic does both. A paper raincoat would go soggy and tear. A steel raincoat would keep you dry, but you could not bend in it.
examples: A child's raincoat for the school walk in the Mumbai monsoon.
A plastic sheet over an auto-rickshaw seat, or over a scooter.
An umbrella made of cloth with a waterproof layer on it.
explanations.art: Four children in the rain: one in a soggy paper raincoat, one in a dripping cotton coat, one stiff in a steel coat, and one happy in a plastic raincoat.

explanations.context: This card is about plates. Different families choose different materials for the same job, and each has a reason.
explanations.description: A plate must hold food. A banana leaf, a steel plate and a paper plate can all do this job. Each one is good in some ways and not in others. People disagree about which is best.
examples: A banana leaf for a meal at a wedding in Tamil Nadu or Kerala.
A steel plate at home every day.
A paper plate at a birthday party.

perspectives.who: A family who eats on banana leaves
perspectives.explanation: A banana leaf is used once, then it goes back into the soil. Nothing is left as waste.

perspectives.who: A family who eats on steel plates
perspectives.explanation: A steel plate can be washed and used every day for many years. It never has to be thrown away.

perspectives.who: People who worry about paper plates
perspectives.explanation: Paper plates are easy for a party. But some have a thin plastic layer inside, so they do not rot well in the soil.

explanations.art: Three plates side by side with rice and sambar on each: a green banana leaf, a shiny steel plate and a white paper plate.

agreed.text: A material is chosen for a job because of what it is like: stiff or flexible, waterproof or absorbent, see-through or not.
agreed.evidence: In the spoon test, steel stayed stiff in water and the paper spoons went soft. The same thing happens every time anyone tries it.

agreed.text: Paper and card are made of plant fibres, and water makes the fibres loosen their hold on each other.
agreed.evidence: At the torn edge of paper you can see tiny fibres. Wet paper tears far more easily than dry paper.

agreed.text: Plastic is waterproof, so it is used for things that must keep water in or out.
agreed.evidence: Buckets, water bottles and raincoats made of plastic hold or keep out water for years.

challenging.claim: Steel is the best material for every spoon.
challenging.who: Many families, because steel spoons last for years
challenging.for: Steel is stiff and strong, does not soak up water, and can be washed again and again.
challenging.against: A wooden spoon is better for a non-stick pan, because steel scratches the pan. A wooden or coconut-shell ladle also stays cool in the hand.
challenging.context: This card is about choosing a spoon.

challenging.claim: Plastic is the best material for keeping rain off.
challenging.who: Many people, because plastic is waterproof and cheap
challenging.for: A plastic raincoat keeps the rain out well, and it is light and flexible.
challenging.against: Inside a plastic raincoat you can get hot and damp from your own sweat. Old plastic raincoats also become waste that lasts a very long time. In Kerala, people once used umbrellas made of dried palm leaves.

big_questions.q: When the card spoon went soft, was it still a spoon?
big_questions.hint: It still had the shape of a spoon. Could it still do a spoon's job?

big_questions.q: Is there one material that could do every job?
big_questions.hint: Think of a towel and a raincoat. Could one material soak up water and keep it out?

big_questions.q: Paper is made from trees, and trees take up water. Does paper still behave a little like the tree?
big_questions.hint: The wood of a tree and paper are both made of plant fibres, and both take up water.

big_questions.q: If you could invent a new material, what job would it do?
big_questions.hint: Think of a job that no material does well yet.

story.title: Ammu's Two Boats
story.note: Kochi is a city in Kerala. Ammamma means grandmother in Malayalam. Ammu, Joel and Ammamma are made up.
text: Ammu was six. She lived on the fourth floor of a building in Kochi, in Kerala, with her mother and her grandmother, Ammamma.
In June, the monsoon came. For three days it rained and rained. A little stream of rainwater ran along the side of the building, past the parked scooters.
'Let's make paper boats,' said Ammu's cousin Joel. Joel was five, and he was staying with them for the holidays.

Ammamma showed them how. She folded an old newspaper page, once, twice, and again. Then she pulled the sides out, and there was a boat. Ammu made one. Joel made one too, with a big crease in the middle.
They ran down the stairs with Ammamma's big black umbrella. They put their boats on the stream. The boats sailed! They bobbed past the scooters and the gate. Ammu and Joel ran beside them, laughing.
Then Ammu's boat began to lean. Its sides went dark and soft. It sank lower and lower, and then it folded in half. Joel's boat did the same, a moment later.
'My boat broke,' said Joel. His lip shook.
Ammu picked up her boat. It was cold and floppy, like a wet leaf. She squeezed it, and water ran out between her fingers. 'It didn't break,' she said slowly. 'It drank the water.'

Back upstairs, Ammamma put the soggy boats on a steel plate. 'The shape was right,' she said. 'But paper drinks water, and then it goes soft. A boat for a long trip needs a material that does not drink water.'
Ammamma smiled. 'Look around the kitchen. What keeps water in, and does not drink it?'
Ammu looked. The steel tumbler kept water in, but she could not fold a tumbler. The glass jar kept water in, but she could not fold glass either. Then she saw the empty milk packet by the sink.
'Plastic!' she said. 'The milk packet keeps the milk in. And I can fold it.'
Ammamma cut the packet open and washed it. It was thin and slippery. Ammu held each fold with her thumb while Ammamma pressed it flat. At last they had a shiny plastic boat.
'Now you show Joel,' said Ammamma. So Ammu showed Joel how to fold the second packet, one fold at a time. 'Hold it down hard,' she told him. 'Plastic springs back.'
They ran down again. The rain had slowed to a drizzle. They put the two plastic boats on the stream.

The boats sailed past the scooters. They sailed past the gate. They spun round in a little whirl near the drain, and Joel shouted. Ammu caught them both before they went down the drain. They were wet outside, but not soft at all.
Ammu yawned. 'Paper for drawing,' she said sleepily. 'Plastic for boats. Steel for spoons. And palm leaves for umbrellas.'
'Every job has its own material,' said Ammamma, and she switched off the light.
story.epiphany: The paper boat had the right shape, but paper drinks water and goes soft. The plastic boat had the same shape and kept the water out. A thing needs the right shape and the right material.
ask: Why did Ammu's paper boat sink?
Why did the plastic boat keep sailing?
What would happen to a boat made of a cotton hanky?
art: A girl and a small boy in a fourth-floor flat in Kochi, watching heavy monsoon rain from the window.
A grandmother folding a newspaper boat at a table, with the two children watching closely.
Two paper boats sailing on a stream of rainwater along the side of a building, past parked scooters.
A soggy paper boat folded in half in the water, and the girl squeezing water out of it.
The girl holding down the folds of a cut-open milk packet while her grandmother presses it flat.
Two shiny plastic boats spinning in a little whirl of rainwater, with the boy shouting with joy.

games.title: Job and Material Pairs
games.players: 2 to 4 players. A grown-up can play too.
games.context: This is a memory game with pairs of cards. One card shows a job. Its partner shows the material for that job. You keep a pair only if you can say why the material suits the job.

printables.title: 16 cards: 8 job cards and 8 material cards
items: JOB: Keep the rain off you (draw rain falling on a child)
MATERIAL: Plastic raincoat (draw a yellow raincoat)
JOB: Eat hot rasam rice (draw a bowl with steam)
MATERIAL: Steel spoon (draw a shiny spoon)
JOB: Dry your wet hands (draw dripping hands)
JOB: See the birds outside (draw a crow on a ledge)
JOB: Draw a picture (draw a crayon)
MATERIAL: Paper (draw a sheet of paper)
JOB: Carry water from the tap (draw a tap)
MATERIAL: Plastic or steel bucket (draw a bucket)
JOB: Hold rice and sambar at a feast (draw rice)
MATERIAL: Banana leaf (draw a green leaf)
JOB: Keep you warm on a cold night (draw the moon)

rules: Print the 16 cards and cut them out. On each card, draw what the brackets say, so you can play without reading.
Mix the cards and lay them face down in 4 rows of 4.
On your turn, turn over two cards.
If they are a job and its material, say why that material suits the job. If you can say why, keep the pair.
If they do not match, turn them face down again. The next player has a turn.
When all the cards are gone, the player with the most pairs wins. If you have the same number, you both win.
With 2 players, a parent and a child take turns. With 4, everyone takes turns in a circle.

setup.art: Sixteen small printed cards face down on a mat in four rows of four.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the cards face down in 4 rows.

setup.art: A girl turning over two cards, one showing rain on a child and one showing a yellow raincoat, and smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Turn two cards. Is it a job and its material?

flow.do: 1. Show your child the cards face up. 2. Read each job and each material together.
flow.say: Each job card has a partner. The partner is the material for that job. Can you find the partner for 'Keep the rain off you'?
flow.kid: Look at the cards. Find the partner for the rain card.

ask.q: Which material keeps the rain off?
good: The plastic raincoat.
Plastic, because water cannot get through.

flow.do: 1. Mix the cards and lay them face down. 2. Take turns. 3. Before a pair is kept, the player says why.
flow.say: You found steel spoon and hot rasam. Why is steel good for hot rasam?
flow.kid: Turn two cards. Is it a pair? Say why.

ask.q: Why is steel good for hot rasam?
good: It stays stiff in hot food.
It does not go soft in water.

flow.parent: Accept any true reason. If a reason is wrong, ask a question that leads to the right one, such as 'What would a paper spoon do in hot rasam?'

flow.do: Count the pairs. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Which job was hardest to find a reason for? Let's think about it together.
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Which one was hardest?

check.q: Which material is right for drying wet hands?
check.why: A cotton towel absorbs water. A plastic bag and a steel plate do not soak up water, so they only push it around.

games.title: Raindrop Hop
games.players: 2 or more players. One person is the caller, and you swap after 6 cards.
games.context: This is a moving game. Four material signs lie on the floor. The caller says a job, and you hop to the material that suits it.

items.b: Steel: it stays stiff in hot food.

items.f: Keep a school bag dry in the rain

items.b: Paper: you can fold it and draw on it.
Steel: a knife must be stiff and sharp.
Plastic or steel: both keep water in.

items.f: Dry your hair after a bath
items.b: Cloth: a towel soaks up water.

items.f: Write a list for the shop
items.b: Paper: you can write on it.

items.f: Cover a scooter seat in the rain

items.b: Cloth: it is soft and flexible, so your fingers can move it.
Paper: it folds well and you can draw on it.

items.f: Make a pot that goes on the stove
items.b: Steel: it does not melt or burn on the flame.

rules: Print the four signs and lay them on the floor, a big step apart.
Print the 12 job cards. One player is the caller and holds them. The other players stand in the middle.
The caller reads a job card out loud.
Each other player hops to the material that suits the job, and says why.
The caller reads the back of the card. A player with a good reason gets one point.
Some jobs have two right answers. If you can say why, you get the point.
After 6 cards, swap: a new player becomes the caller and reads the other 6 cards.
When the last card is done, add up the points. The player with the most points wins. If you have the same number, you both win.

setup.art: Four sheets of paper on a living room floor with a spoon, a raincoat, a towel and a book drawn on them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the four signs on the floor.

setup.art: A girl hopping onto the sheet with a towel on it while a grown-up reads a card.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the job. Hop to the right material.

flow.do: 1. Lay the four printed signs on the floor. 2. Name each one with your child.
flow.say: When I say a job, hop to the material for that job. Then tell me why.
flow.kid: Listen to the job. Hop to the right material. Say why.

flow.do: Read the job cards one by one. After each hop, ask why, then read the back.
flow.say: Wipe up spilt milk! Where did you hop? Why that one?
flow.kid: Hop! Why did you choose that one?

good: Cloth soaks it up.
It absorbs the milk.

flow.parent: For 'Carry water to the plants', both steel and plastic are right. Ask your child why either works.

flow.do: Count the points together.
flow.say: Which job had two right answers?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which job had two answers?

experiments.title: The Spoon Test: which spoon still works after a bath?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make two spoons, one from newspaper and one from card. You carry water with them and with a steel spoon. Then you leave all three in water, and try to stir thick curd.
experiments.question: Why are spoons made of steel? Would a spoon made of paper or card work just as well?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After three minutes in water, which spoon will still stir thick curd? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three spoons are about the same length. Each one carries five scoops of water. Then all three sit in the same bowl of water for the same time. If you add two more minutes, all three get them. Only the material is different.
results_table: After 3 minutes in water: can it stir curd?

materials.item: a steel spoon
half a sheet of newspaper
a strip of thin plain brown card from an empty biscuit or cereal box (not shiny), about 3 fingers wide and as long as the steel spoon
sticky tape
two bowls: one half full of water, one empty
a small bowl of thick curd, or a spoonful of atta mixed with a little water into a thick paste
scissors, for the grown-up
a plastic spoon, if you have one

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up uses the scissors.

schedule.what: Make a newspaper spoon and a card spoon. Carry water with all three spoons. Leave them in water for three minutes. Try to stir thick curd with each.

experiments.record: Draw the three spoons after their bath, side by side. Draw a tick next to each spoon that could still stir the curd, and a cross next to each one that could not.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: After 3 minutes in water: can it stir curd?
rows: A little damp at the edges
No. It went soft and bent over.
Dripped, and went dark and soft
No. It folded up at once.

setup.art: A woman's hands folding half a sheet of newspaper into a thick strip and bending one end up into a small scoop, with tape.
setup.caption: 1. Fold newspaper into a spoon. Cut a card strip and bend its end into a scoop.

setup.art: A girl scooping water from one bowl to another with a card spoon, with a steel spoon and a newspaper spoon waiting on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Carry five scoops of water with each spoon.

setup.art: Three spoons, steel, card and newspaper, standing in a bowl of water.
setup.caption: 3. Leave all three spoons in water for three minutes.

setup.art: A girl pushing a soft, bent card spoon into a bowl of thick curd, next to a steel spoon standing straight in the curd.
setup.caption: 4. Try to stir thick curd with each spoon.

flow.do: 1. Fold the newspaper four times into a thick strip. 2. Bend one end up and tape it into a small scoop. 3. Your grown-up cuts the card strip. 4. Bend its end up the same way and tape it.
flow.say: We are making two new spoons. One is newspaper and one is card. What are they made of? What is our steel spoon made of?
flow.kid: Watch the spoons being made. One is paper. One is card.

ask.q: What is each spoon made of?
good: Newspaper, card and steel.
Two are paper and one is metal.

flow.parent: The spoons need not be neat. Make each one about as long as the steel spoon.

flow.do: 1. Put the three spoons in a row. 2. Ask your child to guess. 3. Draw each guess in the table, or write it for them.
flow.say: Soon all three spoons will sit in water for three minutes. Then we will stir thick curd. Which spoons will still stir it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which spoon will still stir curd after a bath in water? Why?

good: Steel, because it is hard.
The paper ones will go soggy.
The card is thick, so it might work.

flow.parent: Wait for a reason as well as a guess. Any guess is fine. Do not say the answer.

flow.do: 1. Your child carries five scoops of water from the full bowl to the empty bowl, with each spoon. 2. After each spoon, look at it and feel it.
flow.say: Carry five scoops with each spoon. Count with me. Now feel the spoon. Is it the same as before?
flow.kid: Carry five scoops of water with each spoon. Feel each spoon. Is it the same?

good: The newspaper one dripped and went soft.
The card one got a bit wet.
The steel one is the same.

flow.parent: The newspaper spoon drips and darkens at once. The card spoon usually still works for five scoops, with damp edges. The steel spoon does not change.

flow.do: 1. Stand all three spoons in the bowl of water. 2. Wait three minutes. 3. While you wait, sing a song or count to 100 together.
flow.say: Now the spoons have a bath. We wait for three minutes. What do you think is happening to them?
flow.kid: Put all three spoons in the water. Wait and watch.
flow.parent: Push the paper spoons down so their scoops stay under the water.

flow.do: 1. Take out each spoon. 2. Your child tries to stir the thick curd with each one. 3. Mark a tick or a cross in the table.
flow.say: Now stir the curd with each spoon. Which one still works?
flow.kid: Stir the curd with each spoon. Which one still works?

good: The steel spoon stirred the curd.
The card spoon bent over.
The newspaper spoon folded up.

flow.parent: The card should now be soft and bend in the curd. A thin newspaper strip folded four times may take longer than card to go soft. If either paper spoon is still stiff, put all three spoons back in the water for two more minutes, the steel spoon too so it stays fair, and try again. Shiny card with a plastic coating stays stiff much longer, so use plain card. If you have a plastic spoon, test it too. It works like the steel spoon.

flow.do: 1. Tear the edge of the soft card spoon. 2. Look at the torn edge together.
flow.say: Look at the torn edge. Can you see tiny hairs? Why do you think the card went soft, and the steel did not?
flow.kid: Look at the torn edge. Can you see tiny hairs? Why did the card go soft?

ask.q: Why did the card go soft?
good: It drank the water.
Water went inside it.
The steel does not drink water.

flow.parent: Only after your child has given a reason, read the card 'Why water makes paper soft'. Card is made of tiny plant threads called fibres. Water gets between them, and they loosen their hold.

check.q: Which spoon could still stir the curd after three minutes in water?
check.why: Steel does not soak up water, so it stays stiff. The newspaper and the card soaked up water and went soft. If a paper spoon was slow to go soft, it still goes soft with more time.

activities.title: The Biscuit in the Rain: which wrapper keeps it dry?
activities.context: In this activity you wrap biscuits in plastic, paper and cloth. Then you make it rain on them with a spoon of water, and see which biscuit stays driest.

materials.item: 4 plain biscuits, such as Marie biscuits
a piece of a clean plastic bag, cut open flat
a paper napkin or a piece of newspaper
a cotton hanky or a scrap of cotton cloth
a steel plate or a tray
a tumbler of water and a spoon

activities.safety: Keep the plastic bag away from faces.

schedule.what: Wrap three biscuits, leave one bare, sprinkle water over them, and unwrap to see which stayed driest.

activities.record: Draw the four biscuits after the rain. Colour the wet parts blue. Draw a smiley face on the biscuit that stayed driest.

setup.art: Four biscuits on a steel plate: one wrapped in a piece of plastic bag, one in a paper napkin, one in a cotton hanky, and one bare.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap three biscuits. Leave one bare.

setup.art: A small boy dipping his fingers in a tumbler and flicking drops of water over the wrapped biscuits.
setup.caption: 2. Make it rain with your fingers.

setup.art: The unwrapped biscuits: a dry one from the plastic, a slightly damp one from the hanky, a softer damp one from the paper napkin and a wet-patched bare one.
setup.caption: 3. Unwrap. Which biscuit is dry?

flow.do: 1. Wrap one biscuit in plastic, one in paper and one in cloth. 2. Tuck the edges underneath. 3. Leave the fourth biscuit bare.
flow.say: Each biscuit has a coat on. One coat is plastic, one is paper and one is cloth. One biscuit has no coat. Which biscuit will stay dry in the rain? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Each biscuit has a coat. Which one will stay dry? Why?

good: The plastic one, because water slides off plastic.
The cloth one, because it is thick.

flow.parent: Wait for a guess and a reason before you start the rain.

flow.do: 1. Stand the four biscuits on the plate. 2. Your child sprinkles three spoonfuls of water, slowly, over each biscuit. 3. Wait two minutes.
flow.say: Now it is raining! Three spoonfuls for each biscuit. Let's count.
flow.kid: Make it rain! Sprinkle three spoonfuls of water on each biscuit.
flow.parent: Give each biscuit the same rain, from the same height. That way, only the coat is different.

flow.do: 1. Wipe the water off each wrapper. 2. Unwrap each biscuit. 3. Your child touches each one and says if it is dry, damp or soggy.
flow.say: Let's open the coats. Touch each biscuit. Is it dry, damp or soggy?
flow.kid: Open each coat. Touch the biscuit. Is it dry or wet?

good: The one in plastic.
Plastic kept the rain out.

flow.parent: The biscuit in plastic should be the driest. The paper and the hanky let some water through, so those biscuits are usually damp, and the paper one is often the softest. The bare one has wet, soft patches. How wet each one gets depends on how much water went on, so compare the biscuits with each other. If the plastic has a gap, water runs in.

flow.do: Talk about raincoats. Then eat the driest biscuit, if it is dry and clean, and put the wet ones in the bin.
flow.say: Which coat would you want in the rain? Why is a raincoat made of plastic?
flow.kid: Which coat would you wear in the rain? Why?

ask.q: Why is a raincoat made of plastic?
good: Plastic keeps the water out.
It is waterproof.
Paper and cloth let the water in.

check.q: Which wrapper kept the biscuit driest?
check.why: Plastic is waterproof, so the rain could not get through. The paper and the cloth absorbed the water and let it reach the biscuit.

activities.title: Mop the Spill: which material soaks up water?
activities.context: In this activity you spill a little water on a plate, and try to wipe it up with plastic, foil, paper and cloth. You find out why a towel is made of cloth.

materials.item: a steel plate
a spoon and a tumbler of water
a piece of a plastic bag, about the size of your hand
a piece of kitchen foil, the same size
a piece of newspaper, the same size
a piece of cotton cloth, the same size

schedule.what: Spill one spoon of water four times, and try to mop each spill with a different material.

activities.record: Draw the four materials in a row. Under each one, draw a full drop if it soaked up the water, and an empty circle if it did not.

setup.art: Four small squares on a table, a plastic bag piece, a foil piece, a newspaper piece and a cotton cloth, next to a steel plate with a puddle of water.
setup.caption: 1. Put one spoon of water on the plate.

setup.art: A girl pressing a cotton cloth on a puddle on a steel plate, the cloth going dark as it soaks up the water.
setup.caption: 2. Press each material on the spill. Did the water go?

flow.do: 1. Pour one spoon of water onto the plate. 2. Show the four materials.
flow.say: Oh no, a spill! Which of these will wipe it up best? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which one will wipe up the water best? Why?

good: The cloth, because towels are cloth.
The paper, because paper gets wet.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses one material on the spill and lifts it. 2. Look at the plate. 3. Wipe the plate dry, pour a new spoon of water, and try the next material.
flow.say: Press it down and lift it up. Is the water still on the plate?
flow.kid: Press it on the water. Lift it. Where did the water go?

good: The plastic and foil just pushed the water about.
The cloth and paper soaked it up.

flow.parent: Plastic and foil only push the water around. Cloth and paper absorb it. Cloth usually holds more without tearing.

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: Plastic was good for the biscuit's coat, but bad for mopping. Why?
flow.kid: Plastic kept the biscuit dry. But it could not mop. Why?

good: Plastic does not soak up water.
A raincoat must keep water out, but a towel must soak it up.

flow.parent: This is the key idea. Being waterproof is right for a raincoat and wrong for a towel. The job decides which material is right.

activities.title: Hold Hands Like Paper
activities.context: This is an acting game for two or more people. You hold hands like the tiny threads in paper. Then you find out what water does to those threads.

materials.item: a small bowl of water

schedule.what: Act out dry paper, wet paper and steel.

activities.record: Draw yourselves holding hands as dry paper threads, and again as wet paper threads.

setup.art: A grown-up and a girl standing in a line holding hands tightly, with a sign saying DRY PAPER.
setup.caption: 1. Hold hands tightly. You are dry paper threads.

setup.art: The same two people holding hands loosely with only fingertips, while water drops are drawn falling on them, and a sign saying WET PAPER.
setup.caption: 2. Water comes! Hold only with your fingertips.

flow.do: 1. Stand in a line with your child and anyone else at home. 2. Hold hands tightly.
flow.say: We are the tiny threads inside a piece of paper. Dry threads hold on to each other tightly. Can anyone pull us apart?
flow.kid: Hold hands tight. You are threads in dry paper.
flow.parent: Let your child try to pull the line apart gently. It is hard.

flow.do: 1. Flick a few drops of water on everyone's hands. 2. Now hold on with fingertips only. 3. Your child gives the line a gentle push.
flow.say: Water is coming in between us! Now we can only hold with our fingertips. Push gently. What happens?
flow.kid: Water came in! Hold with your fingertips. Push. What happens?

good: The line came apart.
It was easy to break.

flow.parent: This is what happens inside the card spoon in the Spoon Test, and inside a paper boat in a puddle.

flow.do: 1. Now hold each other by the elbows, arms locked. 2. Flick water again. 3. Push gently.
flow.say: Now we are steel. Steel does not let water inside. Water lands on us, but we keep holding. Push. Did we come apart?
flow.kid: Now you are steel. Lock arms. Water cannot get in. Push!

good: Water could not get in between.
Steel does not soak up water.

projects.title: My Book of Right Materials
projects.context: In this project you make a small book. On each page you draw one thing from your home, its job, and its material. On the last page, you draw a silly swap.

materials.item: 2 sheets of paper, folded in half twice and stapled into a small book
crayons or colour pencils
a stapler or a needle and thread, for the grown-up

projects.safety: A grown-up does the stapling or sewing.

schedule.what: Make the book. Draw two things from the kitchen, with their job and their material.
Draw two things from the bathroom or the bedroom, with their job and their material.
Draw a silly swap: a thing made of the wrong material. Show the book to the family.

projects.record: A small book with a drawing on each page. Each drawing has the thing, its job, and its material. The last page has a silly swap.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper folded into a small book, held by a stapler, with a girl writing her name on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Fold two sheets into a little book.

setup.art: An open little book showing a drawing of a steel spoon with a bowl of rice, and the words 'carries food' and 'steel'.
setup.caption: 2. On each page, draw a thing, its job, and its material.

flow.do: 1. Fold and staple the book. 2. Your child chooses two things in the kitchen. 3. They draw each one on its own page.
flow.say: What does this thing do? What is it made of? Why is that the right material for its job?
flow.kid: Draw a thing from the kitchen. What job does it do? What is it made of?

good: It holds water and does not break.
It does not soak up water.

flow.parent: Write the job and the material under each drawing, in your child's words.

flow.do: Your child chooses two more things, from the bathroom or the bedroom, and draws them.
flow.say: Look at a bucket and a towel. Why is the bucket plastic and the towel cloth?
flow.kid: Draw two more things. Why is each one made of its material?
flow.wait: Do this on the next day.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a silly swap on the last page, such as a glass pillow or a woollen spoon. 2. They show the whole book to the family.
flow.say: Draw something made of the wrong material. What would go wrong?
flow.kid: Draw a silly swap. What goes wrong?

ask.q: What would go wrong with a glass pillow?
good: It would be hard and hurt your head.
It could break.

flow.wait: Do this on the third day.
flow.parent: Write the swap and what goes wrong under the drawing, in your child's words.

challenges.title: Make a Spoon That Works
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a spoon from things at home, but not from metal or plastic spoons. It must carry water without going soft.
challenges.problem: All the spoons are in the wash! Can you make a spoon that carries five scoops of water and does not go soft?
constraints: Do not use a metal or plastic spoon.
The spoon must carry five scoops of water from one bowl to another.
It must not go soft or bend while you use it.
materials: a big leaf, if you have one
general: Tape a bottle cap to an ice-cream stick. The cap holds water and keeps it in.
In Kerala and other coastal parts of India, people have long made ladles from half a coconut shell, fixed to a wooden or bamboo handle.
If you have a big waxy leaf, such as a banana leaf, fold it into a scoop. Waxy leaves are waterproof, so water rolls off.
creative: Wrap the card spoon tightly in foil, so the water cannot reach the card.
Use two ice-cream sticks for a stronger handle.
Make a spoon from two materials: a foil scoop on a stick handle.
challenges.your_turn: Make your spoon and test it with five scoops of water. Did it go soft? Draw your spoon. A grown-up writes the label for each material and its job.

setup.art: A bottle cap taped to an ice-cream stick, a card spoon wrapped in foil, and a folded piece of banana leaf on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Make a spoon from things at home.

setup.art: A girl carrying water in a bottle-cap spoon from one bowl to another, counting on her fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Carry five scoops of water. Does it still work?

flow.do: Read the problem. Show the materials.
flow.say: We need a spoon that does not go soft in water. Which of these things would you use? Why?
flow.kid: Make a spoon that does not go soft. What will you use? Why?

good: The bottle cap, because it is plastic and keeps water in.
Foil, because water does not soak into it.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds a spoon. 2. Help with the tape, but let them choose.
flow.say: Which part holds the water? Which part do you hold?
flow.kid: Build your spoon. Which part holds the water?
flow.parent: A bottle cap on a stick works well. Wet tape lets go, so wrap the tape round and round and keep it dry. A card spoon wrapped in foil works while the foil has no holes.

flow.do: 1. Your child carries five scoops of water. 2. Look at the spoon after each scoop.
flow.say: Let's test it. Five scoops. Is it still stiff?
flow.kid: Test it. Five scoops. Did it go soft?

good: Yes, because plastic does not soak up water.
No, the foil tore, so the card got wet.

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: What would you change to make it better?
flow.kid: How could you make it better?

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to its material.
items.why: A pencil is wood, which is easy to sharpen. A rubber chappal bends and keeps your feet out of the wet. A pickle jar is glass, so you can see the pickle and the jar does not soak it up. A kite is paper, which is light.
items.art: A pencil, a rubber chappal, a pickle jar and a kite on the left, and the words wood, rubber, glass and paper on the right, mixed up.

items.p: A cloth bag left out in the rain gets wet through.
items.why: True. Cloth soaks up water, so a cloth bag in the rain gets wet through. A plastic bag would keep the rain out.

items.p: Draw a child going out in the rain. Give the child a coat that keeps them dry. Colour the coat.
items.a: A drawing of a child in a raincoat, with rain falling.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a raincoat that covers the body, with raindrops running off it. The child may say it is plastic.
items.art: A blank box with grey rain clouds at the top.

items.p: Colour the things that keep water out blue. Colour the things that soak up water green.
items.why: Plastic and steel do not soak up water. Cloth and paper absorb water.

items.p: Three of these are good for keeping the rain off. Circle the one that is not.
items.why: A paper bag soaks up rain and tears. A raincoat, an umbrella and rubber boots are waterproof.
items.art: A raincoat, an umbrella, a pair of rubber boots and a paper bag in a row.

items.p: Here is an umbrella. Say or write the material of each part.
a: cloth with a waterproof layer, or plastic
items.why: The cover keeps the rain off, so it is waterproof. The rods hold the cover open, so they are stiff metal. The handle is for your hand, so it is plastic or wood.
items.art: An open umbrella with lines pointing to the cover, the thin rods and the handle.

items.p: Why is a spoon made of steel and not of paper? Say one reason, and a grown-up can write it.
items.a: Paper soaks up the food and goes soft. Steel stays stiff.
items.why: A strong answer says what paper does in wet food, such as 'it goes soft' or 'it drinks the water', and what steel does instead.

items.p: Draw a boat that would not go soft in a puddle. Tell a grown-up what it is made of.
items.a: A drawing of a boat made of plastic, foil or another material that keeps water out.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a boat made of a material that does not soak up water, such as plastic, and the child can say why paper is not used.

items.p: Draw something at home that is made of glass. Tell a grown-up its job.
items.a: A drawing of a glass thing, such as a window, a jar or a tumbler, with its job said aloud.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a glass thing, and the child says its job, such as letting light in so you can see out.

items.p: Paper goes soft when it is wet.
items.why: True. Water gets in between the tiny plant fibres in paper, and they stop holding each other tightly.

items.p: Three people in a family in Chennai talk about the best spoon.

views.says: Steel is best, because it never goes soft.
Plastic is best, because it is light and red.
For my non-stick pan, wood is best, because steel scratches the pan.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason about the material, not only its colour. For example: 'Kavya, because steel stays stiff in water. But Meenakshi is right too, because wood does not scratch the pan.'
items.why: There is no one best spoon. The best material depends on the job. A child who sees that the job decides has understood the unit.

items.p: Riya, a girl in Class 1, has a raincoat made of cotton cloth. What will happen when she walks in the rain? What would you tell her?
items.a: The cotton will soak up the rain, and Riya will get wet. Tell her to wear a plastic raincoat.
items.why: A strong answer says that cotton absorbs water, and suggests a waterproof material.

items.p: A towel and a raincoat are both used in the rainy season. Which one should soak up water?
items.why: A towel's job is to dry you, so it must soak up water. A raincoat's job is to keep you dry, so it must keep water out.

items.p: Being waterproof is always good.
items.why: False. Waterproof is good for a raincoat. But a waterproof towel could not dry your hands. The job decides.

items.p: Match each problem to the fix.
pairs: Fold a boat from a plastic milk packet
Wrap it in foil, or use a steel spoon
My plastic bag will not mop up the spill
items.why: Plastic does not soak up water, so a plastic boat floats on. Foil keeps water off card. Cloth absorbs water, so it mops up spills.
items.art: A sinking paper boat, a soft card spoon and a plastic bag on a puddle on the left, and three fixes on the right.

items.p: The handle of a steel pan is often wood or plastic. Why?
opts: Wood and plastic stay cooler in the hand
Steel is too soft for a handle
Wood and plastic are heavier than steel
items.why: Steel gets hot on the flame. Wood and plastic do not carry the heat to your hand as fast, so they stay cooler.

items.p: A raincoat made of steel would keep the rain out. Why don't we make raincoats of steel?
items.a: Steel is stiff and heavy. You could not bend your arms or walk easily.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a raincoat has two jobs: keep water out, and bend when you move. Steel does only the first.

items.p: Which one would make the worst spoon for curd rice?
items.why: Newspaper soaks up the curd and goes soft. Steel, wood and coconut shell stay stiff enough to scoop.

items.p: You want to find out which spoon can still stir curd after sitting in water. Put the steps in order.
items: Try to stir curd with each spoon
Make a newspaper spoon and a card spoon
Leave the spoons in water for three minutes
Guess which spoon will still stir, and say why
a: Make a newspaper spoon and a card spoon
Guess which spoon will still stir, and say why
Leave the spoons in water for three minutes
Try to stir curd with each spoon
items.why: You need the spoons first. The guess comes before the test. Then the spoons get wet, and stirring shows which one stayed stiff.

items.p: One thing can be made of more than one material.
items.why: True. An umbrella has a cloth cover, metal rods and a plastic or wooden handle. Each part has its own job.

quiz.p: What is the job of a raincoat?
opts: To keep you dry in the rain
To help you see in the dark
quiz.why: A raincoat keeps the rain off you, so you stay dry.

quiz.p: What are most spoons in an Indian kitchen made of?
quiz.why: Most spoons are stainless steel. Steel stays stiff in wet and hot food, and lasts for years.

quiz.p: Which spoon is best for a non-stick pan?
quiz.why: Wood does not scratch the pan. Steel can scratch it.
A waterproof material keeps water out. Rain runs off it.

quiz.p: A raincoat must bend when you walk. Which word means bends easily?
quiz.why: Flexible means it bends easily without breaking. Stiff is the opposite.

quiz.p: Why are rubber boots good in the monsoon?
quiz.why: Rubber keeps water out, and it bends when you walk.

quiz.p: In the Spoon Test, Arjun, a boy in Class 1, leaves a steel spoon and a card spoon in water for three minutes. Then he stirs thick curd. What happens?
opts: The steel spoon stirs, and the card spoon bends
quiz.why: Steel does not soak up water, so it stays stiff. The card soaks up water and goes soft.

quiz.p: In the Spoon Test, why does every spoon sit in the same water for the same time?
opts: So only the material is different
So the curd does not spill
quiz.why: If one spoon sat in water longer, we would not know if the material or the time made the difference. A fair test changes only one thing.

quiz.p: What are the tiny plant threads in paper called?
quiz.why: Paper and card are made of plant fibres. You can see them at a torn edge.

quiz.p: Why does a paper boat go soft in a puddle?
opts: Water gets in between its fibres, and they loosen their hold
The boat is the wrong shape
quiz.why: The shape of a paper boat is right for floating. But water soaks in between the fibres, and the paper goes soft.

applications: Kitchens: pots and spoons are steel, because steel stays stiff in hot, wet food. Handles are often wood or plastic, which stay cooler in the hand.
Monsoon wear: raincoats, umbrellas and rubber chappals are waterproof.
Towels and mops are cloth, because cloth absorbs water.
Engineers choose materials for every job, from a bridge to a bus seat. They ask what the thing must do, then test materials to find one that can.

spotted.text: On a rainy school morning in Mumbai or Kochi, children walk in plastic raincoats, and the rain runs off them.
spotted.art: Children in bright raincoats walking to school in heavy rain, with water running off their hoods.

spotted.text: A cook in a South Indian kitchen stirs a pot of sambar with a long steel ladle.
spotted.art: A woman stirring a big pot of sambar with a long steel ladle, steam rising.

spotted.text: At a wedding feast in Tamil Nadu or Kerala, food is served on banana leaves.
spotted.art: A long row of banana leaves with rice, sambar and payasam, and people sitting on the floor to eat.

spotted.text: An auto-rickshaw driver rolls down plastic side sheets when the rain starts.
spotted.art: An auto-rickshaw in the rain with clear plastic sheets rolled down on its sides.

open_questions.q: Can we make a material that is waterproof, but lets your sweat out, as well as cotton does?
open_questions.why_open: Some new raincoat fabrics let a little damp air out. Scientists are still trying to make one that feels as cool as cotton and stays fully waterproof.

open_questions.q: Can we make a waterproof material that goes back into the soil like a banana leaf?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are testing new materials made from plants and other living things. Nobody knows yet which will work best for raincoats, cups and bags.

ask_kids: What is your spoon made of? Why do you think so?
What would happen if your school bag was made of paper?
Why is your towel made of cloth and not plastic?
Can you find something at home made of two materials? What job does each one do?
If you made a boat, which material would you use?

jokes.j: Why did the paper spoon stay home?
jokes.a: It got too soft for school.

jokes.j: What did the raincoat say to the rain?
jokes.a: You can't get through to me!

jokes.j: Why did the towel go to the beach?
Why didn't the umbrella get the joke?
jokes.a: It went right over its head.

jokes.j: What do you call a paper boat in the rain?
Why was the spoon invited to every party?
jokes.a: It was great at stirring things up.

jokes.j: Why did the biscuit hide inside plastic?
jokes.a: It did not want to get into a soggy situation.

maths.problem: In the Spoon Test, Nila, a girl in Class 1, carried 5 scoops with the steel spoon and 5 scoops with the card spoon. How many scoops did she carry in all?
maths.explain: 5 and 5 more make 10. Count on from 5: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.
maths.context: This is about the Spoon Test, where you carried five scoops of water with each spoon.
maths.why_maths: Adding tells us how much water the spoons moved together.

maths.problem: Pooja, a girl in Class 1, tests three spoons. Her newspaper spoon dripped after 1 scoop. Her card spoon went soft after 6 scoops. Her steel spoon was still fine after 10 scoops. Put the spoons in order, from lasting the shortest to the longest.
maths.explain: 1 is less than 6, and 6 is less than 10. So the newspaper spoon lasted the shortest time, and the steel spoon lasted the longest.
maths.context: This is about the Spoon Test, where you carried water with spoons made of different materials.
maths.why_maths: Putting numbers in order shows at a glance which material lasted longest.

maths.problem: In the Biscuit in the Rain activity, Divya, a girl in Class 1, sprinkled water on 4 biscuits. Then she counted the dry ones: 1. How many were not dry?
maths.explain: 4 biscuits take away 1 dry biscuit leaves 3. Those were the paper, cloth and bare biscuits.
maths.context: This is about the Biscuit in the Rain activity, where you wrapped biscuits and sprinkled water on them.
maths.why_maths: Taking away tells us how many wrappers did not keep the rain out.

warmup.q: What is your spoon made of?
Which material keeps the rain out: paper or plastic?
Which material soaks up water: a towel or a plastic bag?
warmup.a: A towel, because cloth absorbs water.

warmup.q: What happens to a paper boat in a puddle after a while?
Name a thing that must be flexible.
warmup.a: For example, a raincoat, a rubber band or a cloth bag.

warmup.q: Why is a window made of glass?
warmup.a: So you can see through it.

founder: ideas/by_topic/materials-and-their-properties.md: the notebook's ideas on knocking wood, metal and cloth, transparency and heat belong to other units. Its 'drama of materials auditioning' idea shaped the Hold Hands Like Paper act-out. The Class 3 unit on this subtopic uses the hot spoon race, woollen socks and the clay pot, the Class 2 testing unit uses a stretch test, a sketch-pen spot test and a paper doll raincoat, and the Class 1 'what is it made of' unit uses the paper cup and newspaper cone. So this unit uses a soaked spoon test, wrapped biscuits, a mopping test and a memory game instead.
Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, Unit 4.2 'Using materials': why things are made of the materials they are, and testing which material keeps water out.
science: Paper and card are mats of cellulose fibres from plants, held together mainly by hydrogen bonds between the fibres. Water gets between the fibres and weakens these bonds, so wet paper loses most of its strength.
Most steel spoons and tumblers in India are stainless steel, iron with chromium mixed in, which stops rust.
Many raincoats and umbrellas are woven fabric coated with a thin layer of plastic, such as PVC or polyurethane, which makes them waterproof.
Harry Brearley's work on chromium steel at the Brown-Firth Research Laboratories in Sheffield, 1913, and its first use for cutlery.

roots.context: We have tested spoons in water and wrapped biscuits in the rain. Now we ask what the spoon test tells us about things, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Your card spoon had the same shape as the steel spoon. After its bath in water, the card went soft and bent. Water got between its plant threads, and they loosened their hold on each other. A shape can do its job only while the material holding it stays together.
deep_truth.habit: We name things by their shape and their job: a spoon, a boat, a raincoat. But the shape is held up by a material. If the material changes, the shape cannot do its job, even though it still looks the same.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Spoon Test, the card spoon and the steel spoon were the same size and shape. After its bath in water, the card spoon bent over in thick curd, and the steel spoon stirred it. At the torn edge of the soft card, tiny fibres could be seen.

three.who_am_i: Your body is made of many materials too. Hard bones hold you up, and soft, flexible skin lets you bend and keeps rain out.
three.what_is_life: Living beings make materials for their own jobs. A banana plant makes waxy leaves, so rain rolls off them. A spider makes silk for her web.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of materials, and each one meets water, heat and pushes in its own way. That is why each job has its own material.

roots.thread: Steel, paper, plastic and cloth are all made of atoms, and the same few kinds of atoms make every material. How the atoms are joined decides how a material behaves in water. Everything is conscious, the plant fibres and the steel too, and each material meets water in its own way.

teachings.teaching: First think: this person can do this job, in this way. Then give the job to that person.
teachings.link: The Kural is about choosing people for work. In the Spoon Test we chose materials the same way. We tried each one with the job before we trusted it.

teachings.teaching: It is better to follow your own nature, even imperfectly, than to copy another's nature perfectly.
teachings.link: The Gita is speaking about people. In Indian thought, the word dharma is also used for the nature of a thing, as burning is the nature of fire. Card has its own nature: it drinks water. Asked to do steel's job, it could not.

science.text: Paper and card are made of tiny plant fibres that stick to each other. Water gets between the fibres and loosens their hold. That is why wet paper is much weaker than dry paper.
Scientists are making new materials that can mend their own small cracks, a little like skin heals. Nobody knows yet how well these will work for everyday things.

other_view.view: Many scientists say that only living beings with brains are aware. For them, the card goes soft only because water gets between its fibres, and steel stays stiff only because its atoms hold tightly.

practice.title: One drop on steel, one drop on paper
practice.say: Hold a steel spoon in one hand and a piece of paper in the other. I will put one drop of water on each. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out. Watch the drop on the steel. Does it stay a drop? Now watch the drop on the paper. What is happening to it? Keep watching for three slow breaths. Where did the water on the paper go?
practice.kid: Hold a spoon and a paper. Put one drop on each. Breathe slowly. Watch both drops. Where did the paper's drop go?

ask: Your body is made of materials too. Which parts are stiff, and which parts bend?
Why does a spider make silk and not paper for her web?
If you could swap the material of one thing at home, what would you swap, and what would go wrong?
roots.art: A girl sitting still, holding a steel spoon with a round drop of water on it in one hand, and a paper with a spreading wet patch in the other.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, steel spoons and knives went rusty and stained. Lemon, tamarind and vinegar left dark marks on them. People believed that steel always rusts when it gets wet, so they dried and polished their knives after every meal. In 1913, in the steel-making city of Sheffield in England, a scientist named Harry Brearley was testing new kinds of steel. He had started work as a boy, washing bottles in a steel lab. Brearley mixed a metal called chromium into steel. Acid marks ordinary steel, but it hardly marked Brearley's new steel. It did not rust either. Brearley thought it would make good knives and spoons. A cutler tested it with vinegar, and it stayed bright. People called it stainless steel. Today, most spoons, plates and tumblers in Indian kitchens are stainless steel.
how_we_found_out.who: Harry Brearley (1871 to 1948), a scientist in Sheffield, England, who started work as a boy washing bottles in a steel lab
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Steel always rusts when it gets wet, so a steel spoon will always go dark and rusty.
